blogs.title: Ondine at the Foramen Magnum: Central Hypoventilation as a Chiari I Presentation
blogs.description: CMI can selectively disrupt automatic (brainstem) but spare voluntary (cortical) breathing, producing central hypoventilation that looks like acquired Ondine’s curse. This post unpacks the neuroanatomy (medullary compression, CSF flow disruption) and the bedside clues: profound desaturations without distress, events triggered by distraction or sleep, and normal lungs. We’ll cover immediate safety steps (avoid respiratory depressants, use nocturnal oximetry/capnography, escalation to noninvasive support when needed), why central rather than obstructive events should prompt brain imaging, and how posterior fossa decompression can reverse respiratory dysfunction.

blogs.title: The Normal Scope Fallacy: When Choking and Dysphagia Are Brainstem, Not Lumen
blogs.description: Equal difficulty with solids and liquids plus normal laryngoscopy and endoscopy should pivot thinking from structural ENT/GI disease to neurogenic oropharyngeal dysfunction. Using this case, we outline a practical algorithm: look for lower cranial nerve involvement, order videofluoroscopic swallow to identify neurogenic patterns, assess for associated occipital headaches or Valsalva symptoms, and image the craniocervical junction for CMI. We summarize prevalence data linking dysphagia to CMI and discuss when to stop repeating normal scopes and start a neurological work-up.

blogs.title: Beyond Millimeters: Reading Chiari I Imaging With Clinical Intent
blogs.description: Tonsillar descent cutoffs (≥5 mm) are crude. What often matters is posterior fossa crowding, CSF space effacement, brainstem kinking, and cine CSF flow—features that can be missed on quick reads and even present on old scans if you look back. This post reviews how to interpret MRI and CT in suspected CMI, the limits of using descent alone, when to add phase-contrast cine, and how imaging features correlate (imperfectly) with symptoms like cough headache, dysphagia, and respiratory instability. We emphasize the value of re-reviewing historical imaging when the story doesn’t fit.

blogs.title: Don’t Under-call It: Interpreting Type III Sleep Studies in Suspected Central Apnea
blogs.description: Type III studies lack EEG, so AHI is diluted by wake time and central events are easy to underestimate. We use this case to show how a low AHI can mask clinically important central instability, why the central apnea index and desaturation burden matter, and when to escalate to full polysomnography with EEG and CO2 monitoring. Practical tips include pairing portable studies with overnight oximetry, recognizing patterns that suggest brainstem disease, and choosing interim support (e.g., backup-rate NIV) while awaiting definitive testing and neurosurgical evaluation.

blogs.title: Did the Crash Cause the Chiari? Counseling Through Acquired vs Congenital CMI
blogs.description: Trauma can unmask or, less commonly, contribute to tonsillar descent. This post reviews the evidence for post-traumatic CMI, the challenges of causality without pre-injury imaging, and the clinical reality that management is driven by symptoms and crowding, not etiology. We offer a framework for patient counseling (including medico-legal nuance), timelines that raise suspicion for trauma-related change, and documentation pearls when a patient’s symptom onset follows head or neck injury.

blogs.title: Silent Suffocation: Why Some Patients Desaturate Without Dyspnea
blogs.description: Brainstem pathway dysfunction can decouple gas exchange from the conscious perception of breathlessness. We explore the neurobiology of interoception (afferents through the brainstem to insula) to explain why patients with CMI may have severe desaturations yet feel fine. Clinical implications include safety planning (alerts, supervised sleep during flares), educating patients to check oximetry during ‘spells,’ avoiding sedatives, and recognizing the difference between this phenomenon and other forms of ‘happy hypoxemia.’
